messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Public Transport: Bus riding, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Anika is a 25-year-old South Asian American woman who works as a counselor, a role she had once experienced as a natural extension of her belief in people and community. Before the incident, she had a busy social life that overlapped with her work; she met friends after shifts, stayed connected with other South Asian young professionals, and moved through the city easily on buses. The event that now divides her life into before and after happened during the day while she was commuting. She was on a city bus when police boarded or stopped the vehicle and a routine interaction turned violent around her. She remembers being forced down low, her body compressed and her face partly covered, the smell of dirt and the outdoor air around the roadside mixing with the presence of officers standing over her. Police uniforms, the confined bus space, and the earthy smell from outside fused into the scene. Even now, those details remain the most potent parts of the memory.

In the first days afterward, Anika found that the memory did not return in a single, stable form. At times she could describe what had happened in a flat, detached way, as if she were talking about something she had only witnessed from far away. She would say the sequence of events almost mechanically and feel nothing, which frightened her in its own way because it seemed unreal, as though it had happened to a stranger. At other times the opposite occurred. A bus engine braking outside, the smell of soil after watering plants, or simply seeing police at a station could bring everything back with full force. In those moments she did not feel she was remembering; she felt she was there again with all of it happening at once. The sound, the closeness, the outdoor smell, the officers’ presence arrived together. Her body would pull into the same position it had been in then, as if bracing and folding in on itself before she had time to think. She described covering her face with her hands almost automatically, the gesture appearing before she consciously knew why she was doing it.

Over the following weeks and months, her world narrowed. She stopped taking the bus whenever she could, rearranging her commute and daily errands to avoid public transport. As a counselor, she still had to move through waiting rooms, office corridors, and community settings filled with unfamiliar people, and she found herself studying faces and body language constantly. She watched for a shift in posture, a certain look, any sign that someone might not be what they seemed. She had come to feel that people could turn without warning, that appearances meant little, and that safety depended on catching the change early. Often her body reacted first: a jolt, a tightening, a rush of alarm before her mind had sorted out what she was seeing. Mirrors became another way of staying ahead of danger. She checked them repeatedly—bathroom mirrors, reflective windows, the dark screen of her phone—to see what was behind her, how visible she was, whether anyone was approaching.

The aftermath also altered how she inhabited herself. She felt dirty after the incident in a way that did not respond to logic. The sense was not simply physical, though she experienced it that way too; it was as if something degrading had been left on her. She withdrew from people she had been close to before it happened, especially those from her social and cultural circles. Seeing them made the rupture in her life feel sharper. She had once felt held inside a community that recognized her, and now she often felt outside it, unsure how to return. Being around people who knew the “before” version of her was difficult, so she stopped answering messages and let invitations lapse. Her single life became more isolated, and the loss was concrete: fewer dinners, fewer family-community events, fewer ordinary encounters that had once anchored her.

Sleep became another battleground. Night did not feel like rest to Anika because letting herself drift off meant loosening vigilance. She lay awake listening, staying alert as though sleep itself would leave her unprotected. By morning she was exhausted but still keyed up, then spent the day scanning again. This was especially painful in her work, where the counselor in her knew how much effort it took to remain present with clients while part of her attention tracked exits, uniforms, reflections, and changes in expression.

What finally brought her to seek help was a recent sequence in which she encountered police near a bus stop after rain. The smell of wet soil rose from a patch of ground beside the sidewalk, and before she had formed a thought, she was bent inward with her hands over her face, feeling the event all through her body. She was shaken by how completely it overtook her and by how small her life had become around avoiding reminders, avoiding people, and staying on guard. What frightens her most is the sense that she no longer knows who is safe and that she has lost not only ease in the world but also her place in her own community. What she hopes for, though she says it cautiously, is to be able to move through the city, do her work, and be with her people again without feeling contaminated, exposed, and perpetually on the verge of being hurt.
